steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on risk-aware navigation for mobile robots in unknown 3D environments, motivating the move from occupancy grids to a physics-based risk framework and listing the paper's contributions.

  - probability of collision = joint probability every cell is free -> highly dependent on grid tessellation size

  - examples in Figure 1: curbs, traffic cones, speed bump, sidewalk, buildings, traffic circle, traffic lights
  - same prior work: path planning more intuitive and meaningful with a physical risk metric
  - but only 2D environments
  - here: adapt to 3D, physical risk-based reasoning for the Figure 1 obstacles

  - ii) generalized risk that accounts for traversable obstacles
  - iii) mathematical formulation of a local risk-aware path planning algorithm in the Lambda-Field
  - iv) demonstration on data acquired in a real urban environment

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Navigating in unknown 3D environments is an important task for mobile robots. Before the robot can move, it has to represent the environment it is in. A well-known and efficient way to map the environment is occupancy grids, which were introduced by earlier work. An occupancy grid gives the robot information about whether an obstacle is potentially present at a given position. But this information alone does not cover all the capabilities the robot has to maneuver in its environment. For example a wheeled robot can safely cross grasses, a curb or a speed bump at low speed, as shown in Figure 1. So we need a way to assess how hazardous these things are in order to evolve in such environments. Because of this, many recent works have contributed to risk-aware navigation. However another work showed that the Bayesian occupancy grid, which stores the probability of collision of a given position, is not well suited for computing the risk over paths. This is because the probability of collision is computed as the joint probability that every cell is free of obstacles, and so it depends a lot on the grid tessellation size. To get around this problem they developed a new framework called Lambda-Field that assesses physics-based risks on occupancy grids.

- Obstacles and physical risk
  - most navigation methods in occupancy grids: geometric + semantic reasoning for obstacles (curbs, traffic cones, speed bump, sidewalk, buildings, traffic circle, traffic lights, Figure 1)
  - same prior work: path planning more intuitive and meaningful with a physical risk metric
  - but only 2D; here adapt to 3D, physical risk-based reasoning for the Figure 1 obstacles
- Contributions
  - i) Lambda-Field extended to 3D
  - ii) generalized risk that accounts for traversable obstacles
  - iii) mathematical formulation of a local risk-aware path planning algorithm in the Lambda-Field
  - iv) demonstration on data acquired in a real urban environment

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Navigating in unknown 3D environments is an important task for mobile robots. Before the robot can move, it has to represent the environment it is in. A well-known and efficient way to map the environment is occupancy grids, which were introduced by earlier work. An occupancy grid gives the robot information about whether an obstacle is potentially present at a given position. But this information alone does not cover all the capabilities the robot has to maneuver in its environment. For example a wheeled robot can safely cross grasses, a curb or a speed bump at low speed, as shown in Figure 1. So we need a way to assess how hazardous these things are in order to evolve in such environments. Because of this, many recent works have contributed to risk-aware navigation. However another work showed that the Bayesian occupancy grid, which stores the probability of collision of a given position, is not well suited for computing the risk over paths. This is because the probability of collision is computed as the joint probability that every cell is free of obstacles, and so it depends a lot on the grid tessellation size. To get around this problem they developed a new framework called Lambda-Field that assesses physics-based risks on occupancy grids.

Also, in the occupancy grid framework, most navigation methods use geometric and semantic reasoning to handle the obstacles in the environment, like the curbs, traffic cones, speed bump, sidewalk, buildings, traffic circle and traffic lights shown in Figure 1. The same work showed that path planning is more intuitive and meaningful when a physical risk metric is used. However their work was only developed for 2D environments. In this paper we adapt their work to 3D environments and we use physical, risk-based reasoning to deal with the obstacles shown in Figure 1.

The main contributions of this paper are: i) we extend the Lambda-Field to 3D environments; ii) we generalize the risk so that it takes into account traversable obstacles; iii) we give a mathematical formulation of a local risk-aware path planning algorithm in the Lambda-Field; iv) we demonstrate that the method is applicable, using data acquired in a real urban environment.

steps.text:
Navigating in unknown 3D environments is an important task for mobile robots. Before the robot can move, it has to represent the environment it is in. A well-known and efficient way to map the environment is occupancy grids, which were introduced by [1]. An occupancy grid gives the robot information about whether an obstacle is potentially present at a given position. But this information alone does not cover all the capabilities the robot has to maneuver in its environment. For example a wheeled robot can safely cross grasses, a curb or a speed bump at low speed, as shown in Figure 1. So we need a way to assess how hazardous these things are in order to evolve in such environments. Because of this, many recent works [2] have contributed to risk-aware navigation. However [3] showed that the Bayesian occupancy grid, which stores the probability of collision of a given position, is not well suited for computing the risk over paths. This is because the probability of collision is computed as the joint probability that every cell is free of obstacles, and so it depends a lot on the grid tessellation size. To get around this problem they developed a new framework called Lambda-Field that assesses physics-based risks on occupancy grids.

Also, in the occupancy grid framework, most navigation methods [4] use geometric and semantic reasoning to handle the obstacles in the environment, like the curbs, traffic cones, speed bump, sidewalk, buildings, traffic circle and traffic lights shown in Figure 1. [3] showed that path planning is more intuitive and meaningful when a physical risk metric is used. However their work was only developed for 2D environments. In this paper we adapt their work to 3D environments and we use physical, risk-based reasoning to deal with the obstacles shown in Figure 1.

The main contributions of this paper are: i) we extend the Lambda-Field [3] to 3D environments; ii) we generalize the risk so that it takes into account traversable obstacles; iii) we give a mathematical formulation of a local risk-aware path planning algorithm in the Lambda-Field; iv) we demonstrate that the method is applicable, using data acquired in a real urban environment.

References:
[1] A. Elfes “Using occupancy grids for mobile robot perception and navigation” In Computer 22.6 , 1989, pp. 46–57 DOI: 10.1109/2.30720
[2] Yining Shi et al. “Grid-Centric Traffic Scenario Perception for Autonomous Driving: A Comprehensive Review” In arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.01212 , 2023 arXiv: 2303.01212 [cs.CV]
[3] Johann Laconte et al. “Lambda-Field: A Continuous Counterpart of the Bayesian Occupancy Grid for Risk Assessment” In 2019 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) , 2019, pp. 167–172 DOI: 10.1109/IROS40897.2019.8968100
[4] B.K. Patle et al. “A review: On path planning strategies for navigation of mobile robot” In Defence Technology 15.4 , 2019, pp. 582–606 DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dt.2019.04.011

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Navigating in unknown 3D environments is a crucial task for mobile robots. Before being able to move, a robot must represent the environment in which it evolves. A well-known and efficient way to map the environment is the occupancy grids introduced by [1]. An occupancy grid provides the robot with information about the potential presence of an obstacle at a given position. However, this information alone does not cover all the capabilities of the robot to maneuver within its environment. For example, a wheeled robot can safely cross grasses, a curb, or a speed bump at low speed, as shown in Figure 1. Therefore, a way to assess their hazardous nature is needed to evolve in these environments. Motivated by this, numerous recent works [2] have contributed to risk-aware navigation. However, [3] demonstrated that the Bayesian occupancy grid, which stores the probability of collision of a given position, is ill-suited to compute the risk over paths. Indeed, the probability of collision, computed as the joint probability that every cell is free of obstacles, depends heavily on the grid tessellation size. To overcome this difficulty, they developed a new framework called Lambda-Field to assess physics-based risks on occupancy grids.

Moreover, in the occupancy grid framework, most navigation methods [4] use geometric and semantic reasoning to handle the obstacles present in the environment, such as the curbs, traffic cones, speed bump, sidewalk, buildings, traffic circle and traffic lights shown in Figure 1. [3] showed that path planning becomes more intuitive and meaningful when a physical risk metric is used. However, their work was developed only for 2D environments. Here, we adapt their work to 3D environments and use physical, risk-based reasoning to deal with the obstacles shown in Figure 1.

The main contributions of this paper are i) an extension of the Lambda-Field [3] to 3D environments; ii) a generalization of the risk that takes into account traversable obstacles; iii) a mathematical formulation of a local risk-aware path planning algorithm in the Lambda-Field; iv) a demonstration of the applicability of the method, using data acquired in a real urban environment.

References:
[1] A. Elfes “Using occupancy grids for mobile robot perception and navigation” In Computer 22.6 , 1989, pp. 46–57 DOI: 10.1109/2.30720
[2] Yining Shi et al. “Grid-Centric Traffic Scenario Perception for Autonomous Driving: A Comprehensive Review” In arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.01212 , 2023 arXiv: 2303.01212 [cs.CV]
[3] Johann Laconte et al. “Lambda-Field: A Continuous Counterpart of the Bayesian Occupancy Grid for Risk Assessment” In 2019 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) , 2019, pp. 167–172 DOI: 10.1109/IROS40897.2019.8968100
[4] B.K. Patle et al. “A review: On path planning strategies for navigation of mobile robot” In Defence Technology 15.4 , 2019, pp. 582–606 DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dt.2019.04.011
